title: What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
text:
What this is for
A respondent scores 12 on the PHQ-9, a nine-item depression screener. What does the 12 mean? On its own, not much. It means something once we say whom it is compared with, how far it might move, and which side of a decision it falls on. Classical test theory and reliability gave every score one standard error; Information, precision, and short forms let the error change along the scale. This lesson puts both to work on the numbers respondents are given. The example is the PHQ-9 in a UK panel surveyed in the first week of the 2020 lockdown, with a German sample for contrast.

title: What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
text:
Core ideas

A score needs a reference
A raw score becomes interpretable in one of two ways (Glaser, 1963). A norm-referenced reading compares it with other people’s scores; a criterion-referenced reading compares it with a standard fixed in advance, such as the screener’s cut of 10. The Standards ask that users be told what a reported score means and where its meaning runs out (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014, open access, Standard 5.1). Cut scores come later; first, norms.
The standard norm-referenced scores are (Angoff, 1971; Kolen & Brennan, 2014, ch. 9):

the percentile rank: the percentage of the reference group scoring below, plus half of those scoring the same;
the z score, \((x - \bar x)/s\), and the linear T score, \(50 + 10z\);
the normalized T score, \(50 + 10\,\Phi^{-1}(\text{percentile rank}/100)\), which puts the percentile rank on a normal scale. PROMIS reports its measures as T scores centred on a reference population (Cella et al., 2010).







Recall from What is measurement?: if a score is only ordinal, any order-preserving rescaling of it is as legitimate as the original, and only conclusions that survive every such rescaling are safe.



A percentile rank uses nothing but order, so it survives every rescaling and needs no claim about equal units. A linear T keeps the raw distribution’s shape and spacing; a normalized T imposes a normal shape. On a skewed distribution, such as PHQ-9 scores in the general population, the two part in the tail.
Each is a comparison with one group at one time; the Standards ask that norms describe that group clearly and be renewed often enough to stay accurate (Standards 5.8 and 5.9).

Try it: one score, four reference groups
The PHQ-9 sum scores analysed below: UK adults in March 2020, two UK age bands, and German adults in 2012. The table converts one score; the panels draw each group, with a movable cut.


Code
nm_groups = ["UK 2020, all adults", "UK 2020, ages 18–34", "UK 2020, ages 55+", "Germany 2012"]
viewof nm_score = Inputs.range([0, 27], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "PHQ-9 score"})


















Code
nm_rows = transpose(sm_norms)
nm_counts = Object.fromEntries(nm_groups.map(g => [g, Array.from({length: 28}, (_, s) => nm_rows.find(d => d.group === g && d.score === s)?.n ?? 0)]))
nm_table = nm_groups.map(g => {
  const c = nm_counts[g], mo = momentsFromCounts(c), pr = percentileRank(nm_score, c), z = (nm_score - mo.mean) / mo.sd;
  return {"Reference group": g, n: mo.n, "Percentile rank": pr.toFixed(1), z: z.toFixed(2),
          "Linear T": (50 + 10 * z).toFixed(1), "Normalized T": (50 + 10 * qnorm(pr / 100)).toFixed(1)};
})
Inputs.table(nm_table, {layout: "auto", select: false})
































Code
viewof nm_cut = Inputs.range([1, 27], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Cut score (screen positive at or above)"})









Code
nm_bars = nm_groups.flatMap(g => { const n = momentsFromCounts(nm_counts[g]).n;
  return nm_counts[g].map((c, s) => ({group: g, x1: s - 0.45, x2: s + 0.45, pct: 100 * c / n, side: s >= nm_cut ? "at or above the cut" : "below the cut"})); })
nm_share = nm_groups.map(g => { const c = nm_counts[g], n = momentsFromCounts(c).n;
  return {group: g, share: 100 * c.slice(nm_cut).reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) / n}; })
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 460, marginRight: 10, x: {label: "PHQ-9 sum score", domain: [-0.5, 27.5]}, y: {label: "Percent of the group"},
  fy: {label: null, domain: nm_groups}, facet: {data: nm_bars, y: "group"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["below the cut", "at or above the cut"], range: [palette.light, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(nm_bars, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y: "pct", fill: "side", fy: "group"}),
    Plot.ruleX([nm_cut - 0.5], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.text(nm_share, {fy: "group", x: 27, frameAnchor: "top-right", dy: 6, textAnchor: "end", text: d => `${d.group}: ${d.share.toFixed(1)}% at or above ${nm_cut}`, fill: palette.ink}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})























A 10 has a percentile rank of 79.0 among all UK adults, 64.7 among 18–34-year-olds, 90.1 among those 55 and over, and 96.2 in the German sample: one score, four meanings. At 20, the UK linear T is 73.5 and the normalized T 68.6; the long right tail stretches one and not the other. At 0, 28.5% of the UK sample are tied at a percentile rank of 14.2.
In the panels, the same cut of 10 flags 36.9% of UK 18–34-year-olds, 22.1% of all UK adults, 10.5% of those 55 and over and 4.1% of the German sample. Slide it to 15 and the four shares are 18.5%, 10.9%, 4.6% and 1.2%. A fixed cut flags very different shares of different groups.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Respondent A's percentile rank rises from 50 to 60 between two surveys; respondent B's rises from 90 to 95. With the same reference group both times, what can you conclude without assuming the scale has equal units?",
  options: [
    {text: "Both moved up relative to the reference group; nothing about who changed more on the construct", correct: true, why: "Percentile ranks carry order only. A 10-point rise near the middle and a 5-point rise in the tail can correspond to any sizes of change on the construct, depending on the spacing of the scale there."},
    {text: "A changed twice as much as B", correct: false, why: "That treats differences in percentile ranks as equal units. Near the middle of a distribution a small change in score moves many percentile points; in the tail a large one moves few."},
    {text: "B changed more, because moving up in the tail is harder", correct: false, why: "That is a claim about the spacing of the scale in the tail, which order alone doesn't give you."}
  ]
})










Error bands: one SEM, or a conditional one






Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: the standard error of measurement, \(\sigma_E = \sigma_X\sqrt{1 - \rho_{XX'}}\), is the typical distance between a respondent’s observed and true scores, and CTT gives the same one to everyone, whatever their score.



The simplest band is \(x \pm 1.96\,\sigma_E\), the true scores consistent with what we observed (Lord & Novick, 1968). With the PHQ-9’s SD of 6.22 and alpha of 0.92 in the UK sample below, the SEM is 1.74 and the band ±3.4 points around every score: a 12 has a band from 8.6 to 15.4, which straddles the cut.






Recall from Information, precision, and short forms: test information \(I(\theta)\) is the sum of item information, and the conditional SEM, \(1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}\), is small where many informative items sit and grows where they run out. A screening scale spends its precision where it makes its decisions.



The conditional SEM gives bands that change width along the scale, and the Standards ask for the standard error near each cut score (Standard 2.14; Kolen, Zeng & Hanson, 1996, carry conditional SEMs to a reported scale). The PHQ-9’s items have four categories, so the model below is the graded response model (Samejima, 1969), with one slope per item and a boundary between adjacent categories (Models for polytomous responses develops it). All we need here is that its information adds over items, and that it says how much the sum score varies across replications at a given \(\theta\).






If you’ve done Factor analysis II: omega can stand in for alpha in \(\sigma_X\sqrt{1 - \rho}\). It changes the size of the one SEM, not the fact that there is one.




Try it: bands around a PHQ-9 score
From the graded model fitted below. The upper panel is in PHQ-9 score points: for each sum score, the light bar is CTT’s band and the dark bar the model’s, using the spread of the sum score at the \(\theta\) whose expected score is that sum. The lower panel is the conditional SEM on the \(\theta\) scale.


Code
viewof eb_score = Inputs.range([1, 26], {value: 12, step: 1, label: "Observed PHQ-9 score"})
viewof eb_level = Inputs.radio(["68%", "95%"], {value: "95%", label: "Band"})


















Code
eb_items = transpose(sm_items).map(d => ({a: d.a, d: [d.d1, d.d2, d.d3]}))
eb_z = eb_level === "95%" ? 1.96 : 1
eb_rows = grid(1, 26, 26).map(s => {
  const t = invert(u => expectedScore(u, eb_items), s);
  return {s, theta: t, raw: rawSem(t, eb_items), csem: 1 / Math.sqrt(testInfoGraded(t, eb_items))};
})
eb_now = eb_rows[eb_score - 1]
eb_cut = invert(u => expectedScore(u, eb_items), 10)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Observed PHQ-9 score", domain: [0, 27]}, y: {label: `${eb_level} band, in PHQ-9 score points`, domain: [-5, 32]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["CTT: one SEM (score points)", "Model: conditional SEM (score points)"], range: [palette.light, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([9.5], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX(eb_rows, {x: d => d.s - 0.18, y1: d => d.s - eb_z * sm_sem, y2: d => d.s + eb_z * sm_sem, stroke: () => "CTT: one SEM (score points)", strokeWidth: 4}),
    Plot.ruleX(eb_rows, {x: d => d.s + 0.18, y1: d => d.s - eb_z * d.raw, y2: d => d.s + eb_z * d.raw, stroke: () => "Model: conditional SEM (score points)", strokeWidth: 4}),
    Plot.dot([eb_now], {x: "s", y: "s", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})














































Code
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 200, x: {label: "θ (logits)", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {label: "Conditional SEM, in θ units (logits)", domain: [0, 3]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([eb_cut], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(grid(-3, 3, 241).map(t => ({t, se: Math.min(3, 1 / Math.sqrt(testInfoGraded(t, eb_items)))})), {x: "t", y: "se", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([eb_now], {x: "theta", y: "csem", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})









Code
md`A score of ${eb_score}: the CTT band runs from **${(eb_score - eb_z * sm_sem).toFixed(1)}** to **${(eb_score + eb_z * sm_sem).toFixed(1)}**; the model's from **${(eb_score - eb_z * eb_now.raw).toFixed(1)}** to **${(eb_score + eb_z * eb_now.raw).toFixed(1)}** (raw-score SEM ${eb_now.raw.toFixed(2)}, against CTT's ${sm_sem.toFixed(2)}). ${(eb_score - eb_z * eb_now.raw <= 9.5 && eb_score + eb_z * eb_now.raw >= 9.5) ? "The model's band crosses the cut (the dashed line, between 9 and 10)." : "The model's band stays on one side of the cut (the dashed line, between 9 and 10)."} On the θ scale this score sits at ${eb_now.theta.toFixed(2)}, where the conditional SEM is ${eb_now.csem.toFixed(2)}; the cut is at θ = ${eb_cut.toFixed(2)} (dashed line, lower panel).`







Near the cut the model’s band is wider than CTT’s (7.2 to 16.8 at a score of 12); at a score of 1 it is narrower, because a sum at the floor can’t move far. Yet on the \(\theta\) scale (lower panel) the conditional SEM grows with distance from the middle. Both are right: the expected-score curve flattens near the floor and ceiling, so there one score point covers a wide stretch of \(\theta\), and the error in points divided by the curve’s slope approximates the error in \(\theta\) (shown below). A low score is precise about the score and imprecise about how far below the cut the respondent is.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A scale has reliability 0.84 and SD 5. A respondent scores 22, and the cut is 18. Does the 95% CTT band around 22 reach the cut?",
  options: [
    {text: "No, but only just: the band runs from 18.08 to 25.92", correct: true, why: "SEM $= 5\\sqrt{0.16} = 2$, and $1.96 \\times 2 = 3.92$. The band stops 0.08 above the cut, which is one reason to report the band itself rather than only a verdict."},
    {text: "Yes: the band runs from 21.2 to 22.8", correct: false, why: "That uses $5 \\times 0.16 = 0.8$ as the SEM. The SEM takes the square root: $\\sigma_X\\sqrt{1 - \\rho}$."},
    {text: "Yes: the band runs from 12.2 to 31.8", correct: false, why: "That is $\\pm 1.96$ SDs, the spread of scores across respondents, not the error in one respondent's score."}
  ]
})










Difference scores and reliable change
When the question is whether a respondent changed, the score of interest is a difference, \(D = X_2 - X_1\). For two occasions with equal variances, reliabilities \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) and correlation \(r_{12}\), its reliability is \[\rho_D = \frac{(\rho_1 + \rho_2)/2 - r_{12}}{1 - r_{12}}\] (Lord, 1956). The higher the occasions correlate, the less of the difference is true change. Cronbach and Furby (1970) asked whether change should be measured this way at all; Rogosa and Willett (1983) showed that when respondents differ appreciably in how much their true scores change, the difference can be quite reliable. Which applies depends on the data.
For one respondent, does the change exceed what error alone would produce? The reliable change index of Jacobson and Truax (1991) divides the change by the standard error of a difference, \(\sqrt 2\,\sigma_E\), so a change counts as reliable at the 5% level when \(|x_2 - x_1| \ge 1.96\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_E\). The Standards ask for precision data for such differences (Standard 2.4).

Try it: how reliable is a change?


Code
viewof rc_rel = Inputs.range([0.5, 0.99], {value: 0.92, step: 0.01, label: "Reliability at each occasion"})
viewof rc_r = Inputs.range([0, 0.95], {value: 0.70, step: 0.01, label: "Correlation between occasions"})
viewof rc_sd = Inputs.range([1, 15], {value: 6.2, step: 0.1, label: "SD of the scores"})

























Code
rc_now = diffReliability(rc_rel, rc_rel, rc_r)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Correlation between occasions", domain: [0, 1]}, y: {label: "Reliability of the difference", domain: [0, 1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(grid(0, rc_rel, 101).map(r => ({r, rel: diffReliability(rc_rel, rc_rel, r)})), {x: "r", y: "rel", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([rc_rel], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    ...(rc_r <= rc_rel ? [Plot.dot([{r: rc_r, rel: rc_now}], {x: "r", y: "rel", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})] : [])
  ]
})


















Code
md`${rc_r > rc_rel ? "The occasions correlate more than either is reliable, which the classical model doesn't allow (the dashed line is the limit). " : `Reliability of the difference: **${rc_now.toFixed(2)}**. `}SEM ${(rc_sd * Math.sqrt(1 - rc_rel)).toFixed(2)}; a change counts as reliable when it is at least **${(1.96 * Math.SQRT2 * rc_sd * Math.sqrt(1 - rc_rel)).toFixed(1)}** points.`







At the PHQ-9’s values the difference has reliability 0.73, and a change must be 4.9 points to count. Raise the correlation to 0.85 and the reliability falls to 0.47 while the threshold stays put: the threshold depends only on the SEM. Lower the reliability to 0.80 and the threshold grows to 7.7 points, over a quarter of the scale.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A scale has reliability 0.80 and SD 10. How large must a change between two occasions be to count as reliable at the 5% level?",
  options: [
    {text: "About 12.4 points", correct: true, why: "SEM $= 10\\sqrt{0.2} \\approx 4.47$; the standard error of a difference is $\\sqrt 2 \\times 4.47 \\approx 6.32$; and $1.96 \\times 6.32 \\approx 12.4$."},
    {text: "About 8.8 points", correct: false, why: "That is $1.96 \\times$ SEM, the band for one score. A difference carries error from both occasions, so its standard error is $\\sqrt 2$ times larger."},
    {text: "About 6.3 points", correct: false, why: "That is the standard error of the difference itself. For the 5% level it still needs multiplying by 1.96."}
  ]
})










Cut scores are decisions
A cut score turns a score into a category. Where does the number come from? There are two routes, and both end in a choice.
The empirical route sets the cut against an outside criterion. The PHQ-9’s 10 was chosen against diagnostic interviews: in its first validation a score of 10 or more had a sensitivity and a specificity of 88% for major depression (Kroenke, Spitzer & Williams, 2001), and an individual-participant meta-analysis found that 10 maximized the two combined (Levis, Benedetti & Thombs, 2019). An earlier meta-analysis, though, found no substantial differences in pooled sensitivity and specificity across cuts from 8 to 11 (Manea, Gilbody & McMillan, 2012). The data narrow the range; choosing within it trades missed cases against false alarms. Accuracy against the criterion belongs to Validity evidence.
The judgmental route asks experts. In the Angoff method (Angoff, 1971; Cizek & Bunch, 2007, ch. 6) each judge pictures a borderline respondent, just good enough to pass, and estimates for every item the probability that this respondent gets it right. A judge’s cut is the sum of their probabilities; the panel’s is the mean over judges, with a standard error from their spread. The bookmark method orders items by difficulty and asks where the borderline respondent’s mastery stops (Cizek & Bunch, 2007, ch. 10).

Try it: an Angoff panel
Ten Rasch items, difficulties −2 to 2. Each judge’s borderline respondent is scattered around the panel’s, and ratings carry a little noise.


Code
viewof an_n = Inputs.range([3, 15], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Number of judges"})
viewof an_theta = Inputs.range([-1.5, 1.5], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "The panel's borderline θ"})
viewof an_spread = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "How much judges disagree (SD)"})

























Code
an_bs = [-2, -1.5, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]
an = angoffPanel(an_bs, an_n, an_theta, an_spread, 0.05, rng(61))
an_cells = an.panel.flatMap(j => j.ratings.map((p, i) => ({judge: `Judge ${j.judge}`, item: `b = ${an_bs[i]}`.replace("-", "−"), p})))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 60 + 28 * an_n, marginLeft: 70, padding: 0.05,
  x: {label: "Item", domain: an_bs.map(b => `b = ${b}`.replace("-", "−"))}, y: {label: null, domain: an.panel.map(j => `Judge ${j.judge}`)},
  color: {type: "linear", domain: [0, 1], range: [palette.white, palette.main], legend: true, label: "Rated probability"},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(an_cells, {x: "item", y: "judge", fill: "p"}),
    Plot.text(an_cells, {x: "item", y: "judge", text: d => d.p.toFixed(2), fill: d => d.p > 0.6 ? palette.white : palette.ink})
  ]
})
































Code
md`Judges' cuts: ${an.panel.map(j => j.sum.toFixed(2)).join(", ")}. The panel's cut is **${an.cut.toFixed(2)}** of 10, with a standard error of **${an.se.toFixed(2)}**. Through the test characteristic curve that is θ = **${an.thetaCut.toFixed(2)}** (95% interval ${an.thetaLo.toFixed(2)} to ${an.thetaHi.toFixed(2)}).`







At the defaults judge 4 (a cut of 3.41, against 5.48 to 6.10) pulls the panel’s cut, 5.39 (standard error 0.51), down to θ = 0.24, below the intended 0.5. With no disagreement the standard error is 0.07 and the cut lands at θ = 0.50. With disagreement 1 it is 1.01, and 15 judges bring it to 0.50, roughly the square-root law.
Either way, the Standards ask that a cut’s rationale be documented and, where feasible, informed by data on the criterion (Standards 5.21 and 5.23). And a respondent whose true score sits at the cut would screen positive on about half of hypothetical replications; the Go deeper callout turns that into a number for a test.






NoteGo deeper: classification consistency at a cut





Assumptions: an item response model holds with known item parameters; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); two administrations are independent given \(\theta\) (parallel forms, or the same form with no memory of the first); respondents are classified by their sum score \(X\) against a cut \(C\).
Given \(\theta\). Local independence lets us compute the sum score’s distribution at each \(\theta\) exactly, by adding items one at a time (Lord & Wingersky, 1984). Start with \(f_0(0) = 1\); after item \(i\), with category probabilities \(P_{ik}(\theta)\) for scores \(k = 0, 1, \dots\), \[f_i(s) = \sum_k f_{i-1}(s - k)\,P_{ik}(\theta).\] Then \(p(\theta) = \Pr(X \ge C \mid \theta) = \sum_{s \ge C} f_I(s)\), and two independent administrations agree with probability \[\kappa(\theta) = p(\theta)^2 + \big(1 - p(\theta)\big)^2,\] which is near 1 far from the cut and falls to 1/2 where \(p(\theta) = 1/2\).
Over respondents. The test’s classification consistency is the average of \(\kappa(\theta)\) over the ability distribution, \(\int \kappa(\theta)\,g(\theta)\,d\theta\), with \(g\) the fitted distribution, which needs only one administration. Lee (2010) sets out this approach for tests that mix dichotomous and polytomous items. The average is high when most respondents sit far from the cut, whatever happens near it, so a consistency above 0.9 can coexist with near coin-flip classification for the respondents closest to the cut. The Simulate section checks both against two simulated administrations.
Without an item response model. Livingston and Lewis (1995) build the same quantity from classical ingredients: the reliability gives an effective test length, a four-parameter beta distribution stands in for the true scores, and a binomial for the error around them.






What goes in a score report
Reviews of how score reports are designed and read suggest giving the score with its band, the reference group and its date, the cut and what crossing it means, and what the score does not show (Goodman & Hambleton, 2004; Zenisky & Hambleton, 2012; Standard 6.10). A PHQ-9 report would add that the manual treats 10 or more as a flag for a possible clinically significant condition, not a diagnosis (PHQ instruction manual, n.d., p. 2).






If you’ve done Estimating abilities: EAP estimates shrink toward the mean, so averaging them understates differences between groups. That lesson’s simulation makes the point with numbers.



Reports about groups differ: the best estimate for each respondent is not the best input for describing the group. Estimates that borrow from a prior, such as the posterior mean (EAP; Estimating abilities), are pulled toward the centre, most where the test is imprecise, so their spread is smaller than the population’s. Plausible values are draws from each respondent’s posterior instead of its mean; a statistic computed on each set of draws and combined recovers the population’s spread and carries measurement error into its standard error (Mislevy, Beaton, Kaplan & Sheehan, 1992; Wu, 2005). They are for group statistics only.

title: What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
text:
Simulate
5,000 respondents take a PHQ-like graded test twice, with a cut at 10. How often does a respondent land on the same side both times? Compare the model’s prediction (the Go deeper callout) and CTT’s, which treats the two scores as normal with correlation alpha. Base R; seconds.
With the seed as written, 92.7% are classified the same way twice; the model predicts 93.1% and CTT’s normal approximation 90.4%, because the scores pile up at the floor, where a normal curve puts too few. Among the 10.4% whose chance of screening positive is between 0.2 and 0.8, only 55.6% are classified the same way twice. Try cut <- 5 and cut <- 20.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Download this code to run it in your own R session.

title: What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
text:
With real data
The main example is c19prc_uk_mcbride_2021_phq9: the PHQ-9 in the COVID-19 Psychological Research Consortium’s UK panel (Bentall et al., 2022). Wave 1 is an online sample of 2,025 adults with quotas on age, sex and household income, surveyed from 23 to 28 March 2020, the first week of lockdown; 1,406 were followed up a month later (McBride et al., 2021). Its job is to supply real norms, a real cut and two waves. The PHQ-9 asks how often in the last two weeks the respondent was bothered by each of nine symptoms, beginning with “Little interest or pleasure in doing things” (PHQ instruction manual, n.d., p. 5; Kroenke, Spitzer & Williams, 2001). Items are scored 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), none reversed. The code needs mirt (Chalmers, 2012); download it.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/) with a
# CSV download. These links are pinned to one version of the data.
uk_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_4:v7_0.c19prc_uk_mcbride_2021_phq9/rows?format=csv"
de_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_6:v3_4.coroiu_2018_phq9/rows?format=csv"
uk <- read.csv(uk_url)
# Keying: every item is 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day); higher = more
# frequent symptoms, and none is reversed. The panel has six waves; wave 1 is the
# March 2020 baseline and wave 2 the follow-up a month later.
table(uk$wave[!duplicated(paste(uk$id, uk$wave))])     # respondents per wave



   1    2    3    4    5    6 
2025 1406 2019 3867 2520 2058 


Code
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(colnames(wide))])
}
w1 <- long2wide(uk[uk$wave == 1, ])
age <- tapply(uk$cov_age, uk$id, function(x) x[1])[rownames(w1)]
c(respondents = nrow(w1), complete = sum(complete.cases(w1)))


respondents    complete 
       2025        2025 


Everyone answered all nine items. A check against Shevlin et al. (2020), who report that 22.1% of this sample scored 10 or more, with alpha 0.92:


Code
# Check the pipeline against the published figures for wave 1 (Shevlin et al., 2020).
x <- rowSums(w1)
alpha <- function(X) { k <- ncol(X); k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(X, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(X))) }
skew <- function(v) mean((v - mean(v))^3) / sd(v)^3
round(c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), skew = skew(x), share_zero = mean(x == 0),
        share_10_plus = mean(x >= 10), alpha = alpha(w1)), 3)


         mean            sd          skew    share_zero share_10_plus         alpha 
        5.378         6.220         1.291         0.285         0.221         0.921 


We get 22.1% and 0.921. The mean is 5.38, the SD 6.22 and the skew 1.29; 28.5% score 0.

Norms: what is a 10?


Code
predict({
  q: "22% of this sample score 10 or more. What percentile rank does a score of 10 have, and is it the same for 18–34-year-olds as for those 55 and over?",
  choices: ["About the 50th, at every age", "About the 80th, and about the same in each age band", "About the 80th overall; lower for the young, higher for the old", "About the 95th overall"],
  answer: "About the 80th overall; lower for the young, higher for the old",
  reveal: "A 10 is at the 79th percentile overall, the 65th among 18–34-year-olds and the 90th among those 55 and over. The younger respondents reported more symptoms (a mean of 7.8 against 3.4), so the same score is less unusual among them. The table below shows it."
})









Code
# Percentile rank: the percentage scoring below, plus half of those scoring exactly
# the same (the midpoint convention). It uses only the order of the scores.
pr <- function(score, ref) 100 * (mean(ref < score) + mean(ref == score) / 2)
band <- cut(age, c(17, 34, 54, Inf), labels = c("18-34", "35-54", "55+"))
groups <- c(list("UK, all" = x), split(x, band))
round(t(sapply(groups, function(g) c(n = length(g), mean = mean(g),
  share_10_plus = mean(g >= 10), pr_of_10 = pr(10, g)))), 2)


           n mean share_10_plus pr_of_10
UK, all 2025 5.38          0.22    78.96
18-34    626 7.82          0.37    64.70
35-54    763 5.05          0.20    81.39
55+      636 3.37          0.11    90.09


A 10 has a percentile rank of 79.0 overall, 64.7 among 18–34-year-olds and 90.1 among those 55 and over. “Unusual for a UK adult in March 2020” and “unusual for your age” are both reasonable norms, and they give different answers.
The contrast is coroiu_2018_phq9, the same items in German, from adults representative by age and sex, interviewed at home in 2012 (Coroiu et al., 2018). Its job is to show how much a norm depends on its reference group.


Code
de <- read.csv(de_url)
wde <- long2wide(de)
xde <- rowSums(wde[complete.cases(wde), ])    # 43 respondents skipped an item
round(c(n = length(xde), mean = mean(xde), sd = sd(xde),
        share_10_plus = mean(xde >= 10), pr_of_10 = pr(10, xde)), 3)


            n          mean            sd share_10_plus      pr_of_10 
     2404.000         2.290         3.213         0.041        96.215 


Of the 2,404 respondents who answered every item, 4.1% score 10 or more, and a 10 has a percentile rank of 96.2. An earlier German household survey found a similar share, 5.6% (Kocalevent, Hinz & Brähler, 2013). Is the UK’s 22% the pandemic’s doing, then? These data can’t say. The samples differ in country, language, year, sampling (an online quota panel against a household sample) and mode (a screen against an interviewer), and any of these can move a symptom count. What the comparison shows is how much a percentile rank depends on its reference group: the same 10 is the 79th percentile in one and the 96th in the other.


Code
# A linear T keeps the raw distribution's shape; a normalized T forces it to be normal.
linear_T     <- function(score, ref) 50 + 10 * (score - mean(ref)) / sd(ref)
normalized_T <- function(score, ref) 50 + 10 * qnorm(pr(score, ref) / 100)
round(sapply(c(0, 5, 10, 20), function(s)
  c(raw = s, pr = pr(s, x), linear_T = linear_T(s, x), normalized_T = normalized_T(s, x))), 1)


             [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
raw           0.0  5.0 10.0 20.0
pr           14.2 61.7 79.0 96.8
linear_T     41.4 49.4 57.4 73.5
normalized_T 39.3 53.0 58.1 68.6


The two T scores are 49.4 and 53.0 at a raw 5, but 73.5 and 68.6 at a raw 20: the skew separates them in the tail.


Error near the cut


Code
# One SEM for everyone, and a 95% band of 1.96 SEM either side of each score.
sem <- sd(x) * sqrt(1 - alpha(w1))
pos <- x >= 10                                     # screened positive
round(c(sem = sem, half_width = 1.96 * sem,
        positives = sum(pos), band_reaches_cut = mean(x[pos] - 1.96 * sem <= 10)), 3)


             sem       half_width        positives band_reaches_cut 
           1.745            3.420          448.000            0.420 


CTT’s band is ±3.42 points. Of the 448 who screened positive, 42.0% have a band reaching down to 10: the data are consistent with a true score under the cut.


Code
# The graded response model: one slope per item and a boundary between each pair of
# adjacent categories. mirt writes each boundary as a*theta + d_k.
set.seed(61)
grm <- mirt(w1, 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)
round(coef(grm, simplify = TRUE)$items, 2)


        a1    d1    d2    d3
Dep_1 3.24 -0.62 -3.21 -5.61
Dep_2 3.61 -0.28 -3.65 -5.86
Dep_3 2.21  0.05 -2.06 -3.67
Dep_4 2.71  0.08 -2.56 -4.23
Dep_5 2.60 -1.27 -3.09 -4.87
Dep_6 3.39 -1.88 -3.84 -5.95
Dep_7 3.45 -1.48 -3.94 -6.10
Dep_8 3.12 -3.32 -4.71 -6.81
Dep_9 3.36 -3.43 -5.04 -6.94


Code
# The cut on the theta scale: where the expected PHQ-9 score (the test characteristic
# curve) reaches 10.
tcc <- function(t) expected.test(grm, matrix(t))
theta_cut <- uniroot(function(t) tcc(t) - 10, c(-4, 4))$root
csem <- function(t) 1 / sqrt(testinfo(grm, matrix(t)))
round(c(theta_cut = theta_cut, csem_at_cut = csem(theta_cut),
        csem_at_0 = csem(0), csem_at_minus_1 = csem(-1), csem_at_minus_2 = csem(-2)), 2)


      theta_cut     csem_at_cut       csem_at_0 csem_at_minus_1 csem_at_minus_2 
           0.86            0.21            0.27            0.77            2.80 


The slopes run from 2.21 (Dep_3) to 3.61 (Dep_2), all above the 1 to 2.2 where most financial-literacy slopes fell in Information. The cut sits at \(\theta = 0.86\), where the conditional SEM is 0.21; it is 0.27 at \(\theta = 0\), 0.77 at \(-1\) and 2.80 at \(-2\). It is precise where the decision is made and says little about how far below it the 28.5% who scored 0 sit.


Code
# The same precision on the raw-score scale: the SD of the PHQ-9 sum for respondents
# at a given theta, from the model's category probabilities.
raw_csem <- function(t) {
  v <- sapply(1:9, function(i) {
    p <- probtrace(extract.item(grm, i), matrix(t))
    sum((0:3)^2 * p) - sum((0:3) * p)^2
  })
  sqrt(sum(v))
}
at <- sapply(c(1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25), function(s) uniroot(function(t) tcc(t) - s, c(-6, 6))$root)
# The two scales are linked by the slope of the test characteristic curve: an error of
# SE points in the score is an error of about SE / slope on theta. Where the curve is
# flat (near the floor and the ceiling), a small band in points is a wide band in theta.
slope <- sapply(at, function(t) (tcc(t + 0.001) - tcc(t - 0.001)) / 0.002)
round(rbind(raw = c(1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25), theta = at,
            model_sem_raw = sapply(at, raw_csem), ctt_sem_raw = sem,
            tcc_slope = slope, sem_raw_over_slope = sapply(at, raw_csem) / slope,
            csem_theta = sapply(at, csem)), 2)


                    [,1] [,2] [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6]  [,7]
raw                 1.00 3.00 5.00 10.00 15.00 20.00 25.00
theta              -0.48 0.03 0.33  0.86  1.28  1.71  2.33
model_sem_raw       1.03 1.60 1.90  2.36  2.51  2.31  1.49
ctt_sem_raw         1.74 1.74 1.74  1.74  1.74  1.74  1.74
tcc_slope           2.36 5.70 7.67 11.04 12.33 10.90  4.84
sem_raw_over_slope  0.44 0.28 0.25  0.21  0.20  0.21  0.31
csem_theta          0.41 0.26 0.23  0.21  0.20  0.20  0.29


On the raw-score scale the model’s SEM is 2.36 at 10, 1.03 at 1 and 1.49 at 25, against CTT’s 1.74 everywhere. Divided by the expected-score curve’s slope (2.36 points per logit at a score of 1, 11.04 at 10), they become 0.44 and 0.21 on \(\theta\), close to the conditional SEMs of 0.41 and 0.21: narrow in points at the extremes, wide in \(\theta\).


Code
# Bands on the theta scale: each respondent's estimate (EAP, mirt's default) plus or
# minus 1.96 conditional SEMs. How many positives have a band that reaches the cut?
th <- fscores(grm, verbose = FALSE)[, 1]
round(c(band_reaches_cut = mean(th[pos] - 1.96 * csem(th[pos]) <= theta_cut)), 3)


band_reaches_cut 
           0.562 


With conditional-SEM bands on \(\theta\), 56.2% of the positives reach the cut, against 42.0% with CTT’s. Which should a report use? CTT’s band assumes the same error at every score; the model’s assumes its item curves and one \(\theta\) describe the data. At the cut the model’s SEM is about a third larger (2.36 points against 1.74). When a score will be read against a cut, I report the band from the conditional SEM at the cut, and give the one SEM only as a summary of the scale as a whole.


Change between waves


Code
w2 <- long2wide(uk[uk$wave == 2, ])
both <- intersect(rownames(w1), rownames(w2))
x1 <- rowSums(w1[both, ]); x2 <- rowSums(w2[both, ])
r12 <- cor(x1, x2); a1 <- alpha(w1[both, ]); a2 <- alpha(w2[both, ])
# Reliability of the difference x2 - x1 (true-score variance of the difference over
# its observed variance)
rel_diff <- (a1 * var(x1) + a2 * var(x2) - 2 * cov(x1, x2)) / var(x2 - x1)
rci <- 1.96 * sqrt(2) * sem              # reliable change: |x2 - x1| at least this
dx <- x2 - x1
crossed <- (x1 >= 10) != (x2 >= 10)
round(c(n = length(both), r = r12, alpha_1 = a1, alpha_2 = a2, rel_diff = rel_diff,
        rci_threshold = rci, reliable_change = mean(abs(dx) >= rci),
        crossed_cut = mean(crossed), crossed_by_less = mean(crossed & abs(dx) < rci)), 3)


              n               r         alpha_1         alpha_2        rel_diff 
       1406.000           0.703           0.917           0.919           0.723 
  rci_threshold reliable_change     crossed_cut crossed_by_less 
          4.836           0.196           0.139           0.038 


For the 1,406 seen twice, the waves correlate 0.70 and the change score has reliability 0.72. 19.6% changed by 4.8 points or more, the reliable change threshold. 13.9% crossed the cut, and 3.8% crossed it by less than 4.8 points: about a quarter of the crossings are within what error alone could produce. All this assumes the PHQ-9 measures the same thing at both waves, which Invariance and experience asks how to check.


Estimates and plausible values


Code
# Estimates versus plausible values. EAPs are pulled toward the mean; plausible values
# are draws from each respondent's posterior, so across respondents they keep the
# spread of the population.
set.seed(61)
pv <- fscores(grm, plausible.draws = 20, verbose = FALSE)
round(c(sd_eap = sd(th), sd_pv = mean(sapply(pv, function(p) sd(p[, 1]))),
        above_cut_eap = mean(th >= theta_cut),
        above_cut_pv = mean(sapply(pv, function(p) mean(p[, 1] >= theta_cut))),
        observed_10_plus = mean(x >= 10)), 3)


          sd_eap            sd_pv    above_cut_eap     above_cut_pv observed_10_plus 
           0.921            1.001            0.199            0.205            0.221 


The EAPs have an SD of 0.921 and put 19.9% above the cut; plausible values have an SD of 1.001 and put 20.5% above. The gap is small because the PHQ-9 is precise near the cut.

title: What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
text:
Problems

Derivation. Show that for two occasions with equal variances, reliabilities \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) and correlation \(r_{12}\), the difference score has reliability \(\big((\rho_1 + \rho_2)/2 - r_{12}\big)/(1 - r_{12})\) (Lord, 1956). When is it zero? Can it be negative, and what would that say about the classical assumptions?
Which SEM for change? Recompute the reliable change threshold with the wave-2 alpha, and with the test–retest correlation (0.70) in place of alpha. How many respondents change reliably under each? Which would you use, and why?
Old norms. A clinic in 2026 reads patients’ PHQ-9 scores against the UK spring-2020 percentiles. What would you tell them? Use Standard 5.9 and what the German comparison showed about reference groups.
A report for one respondent. Design a one-page PHQ-9 report for a respondent who scored 12: score, band, percentile rank with reference group and date, and the cut. What would you leave out, and why?
Another reference group. Add kohlmann_2016_phq9, PHQ-9 responses from patients with coronary heart disease (Kohlmann et al., 2016). Where does a 10 fall there? Which reference group should a cardiologist use for a new patient, and for which question?
Challenge (open): prevalence from a screener. The cut of 10 was chosen against diagnostic interviews. Should a population survey report the share scoring 10 or more as the prevalence of depression? Think about the positive predictive value at a low base rate. I don’t know of an agreed answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: What does a score mean? Norms, error bands, and cut scores
text:
For instructors

Source: new material, not in EDUC 252: norms, error bands, change scores, cut scores and score reports, following chapters 2 and 5 of the Standards (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014, open access).
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 60 minutes; the PHQ-9 analysis works as a 30-minute lab. The graded model fits in a few seconds in local R.
Changed from the outline: the cut on \(\theta\) is where the test characteristic curve reaches 10. The Simulate section compares the model’s prediction with CTT’s normal approximation rather than with Livingston and Lewis’s beta-binomial model, which the Go deeper callout describes. The German cardiac sample appears only in problem 5.
Held back: the accuracy of a cut against a criterion (Validity evidence); norms on a new form, which need the forms linked first (Equating and linking); whether a unit means the same across the scale (Scale properties); precision at a cut in adaptive testing (Item banks and adaptive testing); estimating \(\theta\) for individuals (Estimating abilities). The fairness of cut scores across groups isn’t treated anywhere in the course.
Item text: the PHQ-9 is in the public domain: its instruction manual says no permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute it (PHQ instruction manual, n.d., p. 8; the PHQ Screeners site says the same). The lesson still quotes only the first item.
Sensitivity: item 9 asks about thoughts of self-harm. The lesson doesn’t analyse it on its own; if students do, a reminder of where support is available is appropriate.
Solutions: held back in solutions/score-meaning.qmd (not published). Problem 6 is open.

Code
import {p2pl, pnorm, grid, loglik, mle, patternsWithSum, expectedPropCorrect, normalQuantiles, palette} from "./widgets/irt.js"
import {quiz, predict} from "./widgets/quiz.js"

title: The Rasch model
text:
What this is for
Sum scores treat every item as interchangeable: a correct answer is worth one point no matter which item it came from. Yet items differ, and the chance of getting any one of them right does not rise in a straight line with the sum score (Where CTT breaks). What is the simplest model that takes items seriously? The Rasch model (Rasch, 1960), with one parameter per person and one per item, on the same scale. That parsimony buys some unusual properties, chief among them that the sum score is all the model needs to know about a person, and it makes demands of the data. This lesson is about both.

title: The Rasch model
The Rasch model
text:
Core ideas

From logistic regression to the Rasch model






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: we regressed 40 chess problems on the players’ Elo ratings, \(\Pr(y = 1) = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)/(1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x))\). Giving each problem its own intercept raised the Elo slope from 0.50 to 0.83. Problem Y15 stood out: about as hard as Y29, but success on it barely moved with Elo. That lesson ended on a question: what if each player had an unknown parameter of their own instead of an observed Elo rating?



The Rasch model is the answer. It keeps the shape of the logistic regression, but everything on the right-hand side is unknown. For person \(j\) and item \(i\), \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \frac{\exp(\theta_j - b_i)}{1 + \exp(\theta_j - b_i)}.\]

\(\theta_j\) is the person’s ability, an idealized version of the sum score. It, and it alone, determines how a person performs on the items. It takes the place of \(\beta_1 \times \text{Elo}\).
\(b_i\) is the item’s difficulty, the item intercept with its sign flipped. When \(\theta = b\), the odds of a correct response are even.

Plotting the probability of a correct response against \(\theta\) for a single item gives the item characteristic curve (ICC). Move the difficulty around and watch what happens.

Try it: an item characteristic curve


Code
viewof icc_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof icc_a = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a (Rasch: a = 1)"})
viewof icc_norm = Inputs.toggle({label: "Overlay the normal CDF", value: false})

























Code
icc_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, icc_b, icc_a), curve: "This item"},
  ...(icc_norm ? [{theta: t, p: pnorm(t - icc_b), curve: "Normal CDF"}] : [])
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: icc_norm, domain: ["This item", "Normal CDF"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: palette.rule}), Plot.ruleX([icc_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(icc_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: icc_b, p: p2pl(icc_b, icc_b, icc_a)}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})
















Changing \(b\) slides the curve left and right without changing its shape: a harder item needs more ability for the same chance of success. The curve never reaches 0 or 1, so nobody is certain to get any item right or wrong. The slope slider is a preview: the Rasch model fixes it at 1 for every item, and relaxing that assumption gives the 2PL, which we take up in From the 1PL to the 4PL. (A challenge, especially if you know probit regression: turn on the normal CDF and find the slope that makes the two curves nearly identical. The answer is roughly 1.7: the scaling constant \(D\) that older IRT papers carry around so that logistic and normal-ogive parameters can be compared. Camilli (1994) traces where it came from.)


Code
quiz({
  q: "A person's ability equals an item's difficulty ($\\theta = b$). What is the probability they get the item right under the Rasch model?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.5", correct: true, why: "At $\\theta = b$ the exponent is 0, and $e^0/(1+e^0) = 1/2$. This is what 'difficulty' means on this scale."},
    {text: "It depends on the item's slope", correct: false, why: "Under the Rasch model every slope is 1. Even in the 2PL, the probability at $\\theta = b$ is still 0.5; the slope only changes how quickly the curve rises around that point."},
    {text: "1, because the person is at the item's level", correct: false, why: "The model never gives a probability of 1. At $\\theta = b$ the person is exactly as likely to get it right as wrong."}
  ]
})










The scale has no origin
Where is zero on this scale? Nowhere in particular. Add the same constant \(C\) to every ability and every difficulty: the model only ever sees \(\theta - b\), so no predicted response changes.

Try it: shift everything


Code
viewof shiftC = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Add C to every θ and b"})









Code
shift_items = [{item: "Easy", b: -1}, {item: "Medium", b: 0.5}, {item: "Hard", b: 2}]
shift_people = [{person: "Ana", theta: -0.5}, {person: "Ben", theta: 1}]
Inputs.table(shift_people.flatMap(pp => shift_items.map(it => ({
  person: pp.person, "θ + C": (pp.theta + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  item: it.item, "b + C": (it.b + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  "P(correct)": p2pl(pp.theta + shiftC, it.b + shiftC).toFixed(3)
}))), {layout: "auto", rows: 7})























The probabilities in the last column do not move. The data can tell us how far apart people and items are, but not where zero is; we say the model is not identified without an extra constraint. Software picks one for you. mirt (Chalmers, 2012) fixes the mean of the ability distribution at 0, as the chess fit below shows. Programs that use conditional maximum likelihood (see the Go deeper callout below) instead fix one item’s difficulty at 0 or make the difficulties sum to 0 (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007). The choice is arbitrary, and results from two programs can differ by exactly such a shift. Remember that before you compare numbers across studies.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two analysts fit the Rasch model to the same data. One reports that item 7 has $b = 1.2$; the other reports $b = 0.9$. Which is most likely?",
  options: [
    {text: "One of them made an error", correct: false, why: "Not necessarily. If one program centers abilities and the other centers difficulties, every $b$ shifts by the same constant."},
    {text: "They used different identification constraints", correct: true, why: "If every item (and every person) differs by the same 0.3, the two solutions make identical predictions. Check the other items before worrying."},
    {text: "Item 7 is misfitting", correct: false, why: "Misfit wouldn't produce a clean shift in the difficulty estimate like this; a constant offset across items points to the choice of origin."}
  ]
})










People and items on one scale: the Wright map
Because \(\theta\) and \(b\) live on the same scale, we can plot them together. A Wright map puts the distribution of people on one side and the item difficulties on the other. It answers a practical question at a glance: is this test well matched to the people who took it?

Try it: build a Wright map


Code
predict({
  q: "Suppose the average person sits 1.5 logits *above* the average item. Roughly what proportion of items will a typical person get right?",
  choices: ["About 50%", "About 60%", "About 75%", "About 95%"],
  answer: "About 75%",
  reveal: "A gap of 1.5 logits puts a typical person at $e^{1.5}/(1+e^{1.5}) \\approx 0.82$ on an average item, and spreading people and items out pulls the average back toward 50%, to roughly three in four. Set the sliders below to check."
})









Code
viewof wm_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability"})
viewof wm_bmean = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean item difficulty"})
viewof wm_bsd = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Spread of item difficulties"})

























Code
wm_people = normalQuantiles(300, wm_mu, 1)
wm_items = normalQuantiles(20, wm_bmean, wm_bsd)
wm_pc = expectedPropCorrect(wm_items, wm_mu, 1)
wm_bins = grid(-5, 4.75, 40).map(lo => ({lo, hi: lo + 0.25, n: wm_people.filter(t => t >= lo && t < lo + 0.25).length}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, y: {label: "Logits", domain: [-5, 5]},
  x: {label: null, ticks: [], domain: [-45, 45]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX(wm_bins, {x1: d => -d.n, x2: 0, y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: palette.light, insetTop: 0.5}),
    Plot.dot(wm_items, {y: d => d, x: (d, i) => 6 + (i % 5) * 6, symbol: "diamond", fill: palette.contrast, r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.text(["People"], {x: -22, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13}),
    Plot.text(["Items"], {x: 18, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Expected proportion correct for this population: **${(100 * wm_pc).toFixed(0)}%**. ${
  wm_mu - wm_bmean > 1 ? "This test is easy for this group: many people sit above the hardest items, and we learn little about differences among them." :
  wm_bmean - wm_mu > 1 ? "This test is hard for this group: many people sit below the easiest items." :
  "Items and people overlap well, which is where a test measures most precisely."}`







Where people and items overlap, the test can tell people apart; where people sit far above or below every item, it cannot. That idea—precision depends on where you are on the scale—is the subject of Information, precision, and short forms.



What the model assumes
Two assumptions merit emphasis (Lord, 1980). First, the formula is right: in particular, a single \(\theta\) drives every response (the model is unidimensional). Second, responses are locally independent: once we know \(\theta\), knowing how someone answered item 3 tells us nothing more about item 4. Both can fail, and it is worth brainstorming how before we meet the formal checks. Two items that share a reading passage? A test where the last ten items measure something else? IRW vignettes look at how often each assumption holds across many IRW datasets: dimensionality and local dependence.


The sum score is sufficient
The Rasch model has a property that sets it apart from nearly every other item response model: the sum score \(r\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) (Fisher, 1922). Once you know how many items someone got right, nothing else in their responses, not even which items, changes what we can learn about their ability.






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: in a logistic regression with an intercept, the derivative of the log likelihood with respect to the intercept is \(\sum_i (y_i - p_i)\), so at the maximum the model’s predicted number of successes equals the observed number.



For one respondent, \(\theta\) plays the part of that intercept. So the maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\theta\) is the value at which the expected number correct, \(\sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), equals the observed number correct, \(r\). Which items make up \(r\) never enters the equation.
That is easier to see than to state. Below are five items of increasing difficulty. Pick a response pattern and look at the likelihood for \(\theta\); then look at every other pattern with the same sum score.

Try it: sufficiency


Code
suf_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
suf_a2 = [0.5, 1.8, 1.0, 0.6, 2.0]
viewof suf_x = Inputs.checkbox(["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 2 (b = −0.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)", "Item 4 (b = 0.5)", "Item 5 (b = 1.5)"],
  {label: "Correct on", value: ["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)"]})
viewof suf_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch (all slopes 1)", "2PL (slopes differ)"], {value: "Rasch (all slopes 1)", label: "Model"})
































Code
suf_pattern = suf_b.map((_, i) => suf_x.some(s => s.startsWith(`Item ${i + 1} `)) ? 1 : 0)
suf_slopes = suf_model.startsWith("Rasch") ? null : suf_a2
suf_sum = suf_pattern.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0)
suf_same = patternsWithSum(5, suf_sum).map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), mle: mle(x, suf_b, suf_slopes)}))
suf_curve = grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, ll: Math.exp(loglik(t, suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes))}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "Likelihood of this pattern"},
  marks: [Plot.line(suf_curve, {x: "theta", y: "ll", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.ruleX([mle(suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes)].filter(Number.isFinite), {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})]
})














































Code
md`Your pattern is **${suf_pattern.join("")}** (sum score ${suf_sum}). The maximum-likelihood estimate of θ for every pattern with the same sum score:`









Code
Inputs.table(suf_same.map(d => ({pattern: d.pattern, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞")})), {layout: "auto", rows: 11})







Under the Rasch model the column is constant. Switch to the 2PL and it no longer is: getting a highly discriminating item right now counts for more. The relationship between sum scores and Rasch abilities is one-to-one but not linear. On these five items the step from 3 to 4 correct moves the estimate from 0.50 to 1.67, and 5 of 5 has no finite estimate at all.
So which should you report, the sum score or \(\hat\theta\)? If the Rasch model fits and everyone took the same items, I’d report the sum score. It carries everything the model knows about the respondent, it orders people exactly as \(\hat\theta\) does, and nobody needs it explained. \(\hat\theta\) earns its keep when respondents take different items, as in Linking and equating: there the sum scores are no longer comparable and \(\theta\) is.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under the Rasch model, two students both answer 3 of 5 items correctly. Student A got the three easiest items right; student B got the three hardest right. What do their ability estimates look like?",
  options: [
    {text: "B's estimate is higher, because B solved harder items", correct: false, why: "That is the intuition the 2PL (and a lot of common sense) would support, but the Rasch model says otherwise: the sum score is sufficient."},
    {text: "They are identical", correct: true, why: "The sum score is sufficient for θ under the Rasch model. B's pattern is less *likely* (it may suggest misfit), but the estimate is the same."},
    {text: "A's estimate is higher, because A's pattern is more consistent", correct: false, why: "Consistency affects how plausible the pattern is under the model—person fit—but not the ability estimate."}
  ]
})










Specific objectivity
The Rasch tradition has a name for the property it prizes: specific objectivity (Rasch, 1977). Comparisons between people should not depend on which items we happened to use, and comparisons between items should not depend on which people happened to take them. It is a demand we place on the data, not something the data grants us for free.
It is easiest to see through ICCs. If two items’ curves never cross, then everyone finds item A easier than item B, whatever their ability. If they cross, the ordering of the items depends on who you ask—and the statement “item A is easier than item B” stops meaning anything on its own.

Try it: do the curves cross?


Code
viewof so_bA = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item A difficulty"})
viewof so_bB = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item B difficulty"})
viewof so_aB = Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Item B slope (Rasch: 1)"})

























Code
so_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bA, 1), item: "Item A"},
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bB, so_aB), item: "Item B"}])
so_cross = Math.abs(so_aB - 1) < 1e-9 ? null : (so_aB * so_bB - so_bA) / (so_aB - 1)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(so_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          ...(so_cross !== null && Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? [Plot.ruleX([so_cross], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})] : [])]
})

























Code
md`${so_cross === null ? "With equal slopes the curves never cross: whoever you are, the ordering of the two items is the same." :
  Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? `The curves cross at θ ≈ ${so_cross.toFixed(2)}. Below that, one item is easier; above it, the other is. Which item is "harder" now depends on the person.` :
  "The slopes differ, so the curves cross somewhere—but outside the range plotted. Push the slope further from 1 to bring the crossing into view."}`







This is why advocates of the Rasch model hold to it so firmly: specific objectivity and sufficiency are what classical measurement in the physical sciences looks like (Wright, 1997). The catch is that the model has to fit. Consistency with the Rasch model comes from hard work—iterative item development and pruning of items that don’t behave—not from applying it to whatever data you have. Whether equal slopes are plausible for typical test data is an empirical question, and the 2PL discrimination vignette looks at it across many IRW datasets.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two items' ICCs cross at θ = 1. What does that imply?",
  options: [
    {text: "The items have different difficulties", correct: false, why: "Items with different difficulties and equal slopes never cross. Crossing requires different slopes."},
    {text: "The items have different slopes, so which item is easier depends on the person's ability", correct: true, why: "Below θ = 1 one item is easier; above it, the other is. That breaks specific objectivity."},
    {text: "The model has not converged", correct: false, why: "Crossing curves are a property of the fitted model (a 2PL or beyond), not a sign of estimation trouble."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: why the sum score is sufficient, and what follows





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; the Rasch model holds for every item; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the difficulties \(b_1, \dots, b_I\) are fixed. Write \(\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}\) (the item’s easiness) and \(r = \sum_i x_i\).
Factorize the likelihood. Using \(\Pr(x_i \mid \theta) = e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}/(1 + e^{\theta - b_i})\) for \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\), \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{I} \frac{e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}}{1 + e^{\theta - b_i}} = \frac{e^{r\theta} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}.\] The data meet \(\theta\) in one place only, \(e^{r\theta}\). The product \(\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}\) depends on which items were right but not on \(\theta\), and the denominator depends on \(\theta\) but not on the data. Taking logs and differentiating gives \(r - \sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), the score equation from the main text.
Condition on \(r\). Add up the probabilities of all the patterns with the same sum score: \[\Pr(r \mid \theta) = \frac{e^{r\theta}\,\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}, \qquad \gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}:\, \sum_i y_i = r} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{y_i},\] where \(\gamma_r\), the elementary symmetric function of order \(r\), is a sum over patterns and contains no \(\theta\). Divide: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r, \theta) = \frac{\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}.\] \(\theta\) has cancelled. Given \(r\), the pattern carries no further information about \(\theta\); that is the definition of a sufficient statistic. Three things follow.

Conditional maximum likelihood. Multiply \(\Pr(\mathbf{x}_j \mid r_j)\) over respondents and you have a likelihood for the difficulties with no \(\theta\) in it. Maximizing it is conditional maximum likelihood (CML). It needs no assumption about how \(\theta\) is distributed, and it gives consistent estimates of the \(b_i\) as the number of respondents grows (Andersen, 1970). Estimating every \(\theta_j\) jointly with the \(b_i\) does not, because the number of person parameters grows with the data (Neyman & Scott, 1948). The wirs analysis below uses \(\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid r)\) to compare the model with the data without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\).
Specific objectivity is a theorem. Take two items, \(i\) and \(k\), and condition on the respondent getting exactly one of them right. The same cancellation, with two items, gives \[\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid x_i + x_k = 1, \theta) = \frac{\varepsilon_i}{\varepsilon_i + \varepsilon_k} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{b_i - b_k}},\] which contains no \(\theta\). Whoever the respondents are, strong or weak, the comparison of the two items comes out the same. Swap the roles of people and items (two respondents, one item, exactly one of them right) and the comparison depends on \(\theta_j - \theta_l\) and not on \(b\). This is Rasch’s specific objectivity, derived rather than assumed. When the model fails, it fails in a checkable way: CML estimates of the difficulties from high and low scorers should agree, and Andersen (1973) turned that into a likelihood-ratio test. Problem 3 tries the two-item version on the chess data.
The converse. For dichotomous items, if some statistic is sufficient for \(\theta\) and is the same statistic whatever the item parameters, it is the sum score, and the model must be the Rasch model: logistic curves with equal slopes (Andersen, 1977). Fischer (1995) collects this and other derivations of the Rasch model. Under the 2PL, the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) plays the part of \(r\), but its weights are item parameters, which is where From the 1PL to the 4PL picks up.







A note on estimation
Fitting the model is harder than it looks, because nothing on the right-hand side is known. The conventional approach, and the one mirt takes, estimates the item parameters first, integrating over the distribution of abilities with the EM algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), and then estimates abilities treating those item parameters as known. Conditional maximum likelihood, from the Go deeper callout above, is the Rasch model’s own alternative. Estimating abilities and Estimating item parameters take these in turn.

title: The Rasch model
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates responses from the Rasch model, fits the model with mirt, and compares the estimated difficulties to the truth. It runs here in your browser; the first run takes about 20 seconds while R and mirt load.
Try changing np to 50, then to 2000, and watch the scatter around the line. With the seed as written, the root mean squared error of the estimated difficulties is 0.34 with 50 people, 0.13 with 500 and 0.04 with 2,000. Now change ni to 40: with 500 people the error barely moves (0.13), because each difficulty rests on the people who answered that item. More items sharpen the abilities instead, which is where Information, precision, and short forms picks up.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

One detail trips up many first-time users: mirt writes the Rasch model as \(\Pr(x = 1) = 1/(1 + \exp(-(\theta + d)))\), so its parameter d is an easiness. Our difficulty is \(b = -d\), which is why the code negates it.
Download this code to run it in your own R session, where you can make the simulation as large as you like.

title: The Rasch model

With real data
Our main example is chess_lnirt, the 40 problems of the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005), which we met in The likelihood and logistic regression; its job here is to show what the Rasch model says about a test built for a wide range of skill. A response is 1 if the player solved the problem. The code below produced every number and figure in this section; download it to run it yourself.

library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)

IRW tables are long, one row per response, so we reshape to one row per player. The first rows above belong to a player with no responses at all; three of the 259 players are like that, and we drop them, leaving 256.


Code
# IRW tables are long: one row per person-item response. mirt wants wide: one
# row per person, one column per item.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
}
resp <- long2wide(df)
# A few players have no responses at all (resp is NA for every item; the first
# rows of the table are one of them). They carry no information, so drop them.
c(players_in_table = nrow(resp), with_no_responses = sum(rowSums(!is.na(resp)) == 0))

resp <- resp[rowSums(!is.na(resp)) > 0, ]
dim(resp)


[1] 256  40




Code
m1 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
# mirt writes the Rasch model as P(x = 1) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(theta + d))), so its
# "d" is an easiness. The difficulty in our notation is b = -d.
b <- -coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
round(head(sort(b)), 2)   # the easiest items

-4.9 -3.6 -3.5 -3.2 -3.0 -2.8

Y36 Y18 Y19 Y15 Y29 Y30 
2.1 2.2 2.7 3.0 3.1 3.6 


The easiest problem (Y31) sits nearly five logits below zero, the mean ability, and the hardest (Y30) more than three and a half above. Is that a wide spread? Wide compared with what? The IRW’s difficulty pool holds Rasch difficulties for 145 IRW tables (Zhang et al., 2025), and chess is one of them.


Code
# How wide is wide? The IRW's difficulty pool (the diffsim vignette) holds
# difficulty estimates for 145 IRW tables and ships with the irw package.
round(c(sd_b = sd(b), range_b = diff(range(b))), 2)   # chess, from our fit


   sd_b range_b 
    2.1     8.5 


Code
if (requireNamespace("irw", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data("diff_long", package = "irw")
  pool_sd <- tapply(diff_long$difficulty, diff_long$dataset, sd)
  print(c(tables = length(pool_sd), round(quantile(pool_sd, c(.25, .5, .75)), 2)))
  # chess_lnirt is in the pool. Compare its entry with the rest of the pool:
  cat(sprintf("chess_lnirt in the pool: SD %.2f, wider than %.0f%% of the %d tables\n",
              pool_sd[["chess_lnirt"]], 100 * mean(pool_sd < pool_sd[["chess_lnirt"]]),
              length(pool_sd)))
  # The pool's chess SD is ours divided by the SD of ability in our fit: the pool
  # puts ability on a scale with SD 1, while mirt's Rasch fit estimates it.
  sd_theta <- sqrt(coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$cov[1, 1])
  cat(sprintf("SD of ability in our fit %.2f; our SD of b divided by it: %.2f\n",
              sd_theta, sd(b) / sd_theta))
}


tables    25%    50%    75% 
145.00   0.70   0.99   1.75 
chess_lnirt in the pool: SD 1.75, wider than 74% of the 145 tables
SD of ability in our fit 1.22; our SD of b divided by it: 1.75


The median table in the pool has a standard deviation of difficulties of 0.99; chess, at 1.75 on the pool’s scale, is more spread out than 74% of them. (The pool fixes the SD of ability at 1, while the Rasch model fixes the slopes at 1 and lets the SD of ability float, here to 1.22; dividing our 2.1 by 1.22 recovers the pool’s 1.75.) That spread is what you want from a test meant to separate novices from masters.
How do these difficulties relate to the simplest measure of item difficulty, the proportion of players who solve the problem?


Code
p <- colMeans(resp, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(p, b, xlab = "Proportion correct (p-value)", ylab = "Rasch difficulty (b)",
     pch = 19, col = "#2780e3")









Code
sprintf("%.4f", cor(p, b, method = "spearman"))   # rank correlation of p and b


[1] "-0.9998"


The rank correlation is −0.9998. That is sufficiency from the item side: with complete data an item’s total is sufficient for its difficulty (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007), and a few missing responses keep it from being exactly −1. The relationship is not linear, though: the Rasch scale stretches out the extremes, where a few percentage points correct correspond to a large difference in difficulty.


Code
theta <- fscores(m1)[, 1]
br <- seq(floor(min(c(theta, b))), ceiling(max(c(theta, b))), by = 0.25)
h <- hist(theta, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-max(h$counts), 12), ylim = range(br), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Logits", main = "Wright map: chess_lnirt")
rect(-h$counts, h$breaks[-length(h$breaks)], 0, h$breaks[-1], col = "#dbeafe", border = "white")
points(rep(1.5, length(b)) + (seq_along(b) %% 8), b, pch = 18, col = "#c2410c")
abline(v = 0)

round(c(mean_theta = mean(theta), mean_b = mean(b)), 2)

Code
# mirt fixes the mean of the ability distribution at 0. Any other origin fits
# exactly as well: add 1 to every theta and every b, and no probability moves.
all.equal(plogis(outer(theta + 1, b + 1, "-")), plogis(outer(theta, b, "-")))


[1] TRUE


The mean ability is 0.00, the constraint mirt imposes, and adding 1 to every ability and difficulty leaves every probability unchanged (all.equal returns TRUE). So the mean difficulty says how hard the test is for this sample: 0.12, about a tenth of a logit, against an SD of ability of 1.22. The test is well targeted.
Does the model fit? A common first look is the infit and outfit statistics (Wright & Masters, 1982): mean squared standardized residuals, which should be near 1 if the model is right. Values well below 1 mean an item is more predictable than the Rasch model expects (typically an item that discriminates better than average); values well above 1 mean it is noisier. How far from 1 is too far is the subject of Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.

Four of the five worst-fitting items by \(|z|\) overfit (outfit from 0.64 to 0.73): they separate strong and weak players more sharply than a common slope allows. The exception is Y15, whose outfit of 2.2 is the largest of all 40 items: by the size of its misfit, it is the worst-fitting item on the test. It is the problem whose success barely moved with Elo in The likelihood and logistic regression. The empirical plot compares the model’s curve with the proportions solved among players grouped by ability. Those proportions barely rise: below-average players solve Y15 more often than the model expects, and the strongest group less often. Why is a question about the problem itself, which the responses alone can’t answer.
For contrast, a table whose job is to show a setting where one ability and equal slopes describe the data less well: wirs, six items from the 1990 Workplace Industrial Relations Survey analysed by Bartholomew (1998). Each item asks whether a kind of consultation took place about the most recent introduction of new equipment (1 = yes), from informal discussion with individual workers (item 1) through joint consultative committees (item 3) to paid union officials (wording from the ltm documentation, Rizopoulos, 2006). Because the sum score is sufficient, the Rasch model says what proportion of respondents with each sum score should say yes to each item, without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\) (the Go deeper callout gives the formula).


Code
wirs_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.wirs/rows?format=csv"
resp_w <- long2wide(read.csv(wirs_url))
dim(resp_w)


[1] 1005    6


Code
m2 <- mirt(resp_w, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
b_w <- -coef(m2, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
# Because the sum score r is sufficient, the Rasch model predicts the proportion
# endorsing item i among respondents with sum score r without reference to theta:
#   P(x_i = 1 | r) = eps_i * gamma_(r-1)(items other than i) / gamma_r(all items),
# with eps = exp(-b) and gamma_r the elementary symmetric functions (see the
# Go deeper callout in the lesson).
esf <- function(eps) {               # gamma_0, gamma_1, ..., gamma_n
  g <- 1
  for (e in eps) g <- c(g, 0) + c(0, g) * e
  g
}
p_given_r <- function(b, i) {        # P(x_i = 1 | r) for r = 0, ..., n
  eps <- exp(-b); g <- esf(eps); g_i <- esf(eps[-i]); r <- seq_along(b)
  c(0, eps[i] * g_i[r] / g[r + 1])
}
r_w <- factor(rowSums(resp_w), levels = 0:6)
tab <- data.frame(r = 0:6, n = as.vector(table(r_w)),
  item1_observed = as.vector(tapply(resp_w[, 1], r_w, mean)),
  item1_rasch    = p_given_r(b_w, 1),
  item3_observed = as.vector(tapply(resp_w[, 3], r_w, mean)),
  item3_rasch    = p_given_r(b_w, 3))
